title: Daily life: read six useful words
description: Read everyday written words in hiragana; meanings and examples appear with feedback.

review.provenance: Independently authored short daily-life cues and explanations; common word spellings and meanings are linguistic facts, not legacy CSV or mock text.
review.rightsBasis: Original agent-written prompts, translations, contexts and explanations; no copied text, audio or third-party assets.

exercises.prompt: At a café, read this word aloud and type its reading in hiragana.

stimulus.context: At a café, ask for a glass of water.

text.context: At a café, ask for a glass of water.

exercises.explanation: 水 is read みず and means water; this is the everyday word for water in a café.

exercises.prompt: On a transit sign, read this place name and type its reading in hiragana.

stimulus.context: Look for the station when taking a train.

text.context: Look for the station when taking a train.

exercises.explanation: 駅 is read えき and means station; it appears on transit signs.

exercises.prompt: In a travel plan, read this transport word and type its reading in hiragana.

stimulus.context: Take a train to the station.

text.context: Take a train to the station.

exercises.explanation: 電車 is read でんしゃ and means train, usually an electric train. Small ゃ belongs to しゃ.

exercises.prompt: Before going out, read this forecast heading and type its reading in hiragana.

stimulus.context: Check the weather before going out.

text.context: Check the weather before going out.

exercises.explanation: 天気 is read てんき and means weather; use it when talking about a forecast.

exercises.prompt: On an errand list, read this activity and type its reading in hiragana.
exercises.explanation: 買い物 is read かいもの and means shopping; the い is part of the written word.

exercises.prompt: In a message about plans for the next day, read this word and type its reading in hiragana.

text.context: A more formal way to say tomorrow.

exercises.explanation: 明日 means tomorrow. Both あした (everyday speech) and あす (more formal or news style) are authored readings here; other readings are not inferred.
